t: What a Bill of Materials Is
name: What a Bill of Materials Is
title: What a Bill of Materials Is
description: A bill of materials (BoM) is a structured list of every raw material, component, and subassembly needed to build one unit of a product. It is the single document that purchasing buys against, production picks against, and costing is calculated from.
how_it_works: Read a BoM top-down: the finished product at level 0, subassemblies at level 1, their parts at level 2, and so on. Each line carries a part number, description, quantity per assembly, and unit of measure.
key_points: One BoM describes exactly one revision of one product.
Every line needs a unique part number - never describe parts by prose alone.
Quantity-per-assembly and unit of measure are mandatory fields.
The BoM is the basis for purchasing, costing, and production planning.
requirements: A defined product structure with unique part numbers for every item; quantities and units of measure; revision control on the BoM document.
standards: IPC-1782 and IPC-2581 for electronics BoMs; ASME Y14.38 for parts lists; company part-numbering standard applied consistently.
citations: IPC-1782 standard for manufacturing data; ASME Y14.38 abbreviations for parts lists.
Lean manufacturing references on material planning (APICS/ASCM body of knowledge).

name: Single-Level vs Multi-Level BoMs
title: Single-Level vs Multi-Level BoMs
description: A single-level BoM lists only the parts bought or made at the top level, flattening subassemblies into their components. A multi-level (indented) BoM shows the full parent-child hierarchy, with each subassembly exploded into its own parts.
how_it_works: Use single-level for simple purchased kits; use multi-level whenever the product has subassemblies built in-house. Indent each level so the parent-child relationship is visible at a glance.
key_points: Single-level: flat list, simplest to maintain for simple products.
Multi-level: indented hierarchy showing subassemblies and their parts.
Level 0 is always the finished shippable product.
Choose the structure that matches how the product is actually built.
requirements: A defined product structure with unique part numbers for every item; quantities and units of measure; revision control on the BoM document.
standards: IPC-1782 and IPC-2581 for electronics BoMs; ASME Y14.38 for parts lists; company part-numbering standard applied consistently.
citations: IPC-1782 standard for manufacturing data; ASME Y14.38 abbreviations for parts lists.

name: Part Numbers and Descriptions
title: Part Numbers and Descriptions
description: Part numbers are short unique identifiers; descriptions are human-readable names. Good practice keeps the part number dumb (no embedded meaning that can go stale) and puts the meaning in the description and attributes.
how_it_works: Assign the next number in your scheme to each new part and record a clear description with key attributes (material, size, finish). Never reuse a retired part number for a different part.
key_points: Part numbers must be unique and never reused.
Keep numbers non-significant; put meaning in description fields.
Descriptions include material, size, and finish where relevant.
One part, one number - variants get their own numbers.
requirements: A defined product structure with unique part numbers for every item; quantities and units of measure; revision control on the BoM document.
standards: IPC-1782 and IPC-2581 for electronics BoMs; ASME Y14.38 for parts lists; company part-numbering standard applied consistently.

name: Quantities and Units of Measure
title: Quantities and Units of Measure
description: Quantity-per-assembly states how many of each part go into one parent; the unit of measure (each, feet, grams, liters) defines what the quantity counts. Mismatched units are one of the most common and expensive BoM errors.
how_it_works: Record quantities in the unit you actually buy or consume the part in, and note the unit explicitly on every line. Convert bulk units (a 1000-ft spool) to per-assembly usage with the conversion stated.
key_points: Every BoM line needs quantity-per-assembly AND unit of measure.
Buy-unit vs use-unit conversions must be stated, not assumed.
Fractional quantities are normal for bulk materials (0.02 liters of adhesive).
Audit units whenever a BoM is copied between metric and imperial shops.
requirements: A defined product structure with unique part numbers for every item; quantities and units of measure; revision control on the BoM document.
standards: IPC-1782 and IPC-2581 for electronics BoMs; ASME Y14.38 for parts lists; company part-numbering standard applied consistently.
citations: IPC-1782 standard for manufacturing data; ASME Y14.38 abbreviations for parts lists.
Lean manufacturing references on material planning (APICS/ASCM body of knowledge).

name: Reference Designators
title: Reference Designators
description: Reference designators (R12, C7, J3) tie each BoM line to exact positions on a schematic or drawing. They turn a parts list into an assembly map: the builder knows not just what, but where.
how_it_works: List the designators for each line, grouped or ranged (R1-R8), and keep them synchronized with the schematic. When the schematic changes, the BoM designators change with it.
key_points: Designators link BoM lines to schematic and layout positions.
Ranges like R1-R8 keep long lists compact.
Quantity must equal the designator count - a mismatch flags an error.
Keep designators in sync with every schematic revision.
requirements: A defined product structure with unique part numbers for every item; quantities and units of measure; revision control on the BoM document.
standards: IPC-1782 and IPC-2581 for electronics BoMs; ASME Y14.38 for parts lists; company part-numbering standard applied consistently.

name: Engineering vs Manufacturing BoMs
title: Engineering vs Manufacturing BoMs
description: The engineering BoM (EBOM) reflects how the product is designed - functional groupings from CAD. The manufacturing BoM (MBOM) reflects how it is built - process order, consumables, packaging, and phantom assemblies added.
how_it_works: Release the EBOM from engineering, then let manufacturing derive the MBOM by reordering for the line and adding process materials. Keep both under revision control and trace every MBOM line back to its EBOM source.
key_points: EBOM: as-designed structure from engineering/CAD.
MBOM: as-built structure for the production line.
MBOM adds consumables, packaging, and process steps EBOM omits.
Traceability between EBOM and MBOM lines is mandatory.
requirements: A defined product structure with unique part numbers for every item; quantities and units of measure; revision control on the BoM document.
standards: IPC-1782 and IPC-2581 for electronics BoMs; ASME Y14.38 for parts lists; company part-numbering standard applied consistently.
citations: IPC-1782 standard for manufacturing data; ASME Y14.38 abbreviations for parts lists.

name: BoM Revision Control
title: BoM Revision Control
description: BoMs change, and uncontrolled changes cause wrong parts to be ordered and built. Revision control gives every released BoM version an identifier and a change record so everyone works from the same truth.
how_it_works: Freeze the BoM at each release with a revision letter or number, log what changed and why, and mark old revisions superseded. Purchasing and production may only build from the current released revision.
key_points: Every release gets a revision identifier and a change log.
Only the current released revision is buildable.
Superseded revisions are retained for traceability, never deleted.
An engineering change order is the only legitimate way to alter a released BoM.
requirements: A defined product structure with unique part numbers for every item; quantities and units of measure; revision control on the BoM document.
standards: IPC-1782 and IPC-2581 for electronics BoMs; ASME Y14.38 for parts lists; company part-numbering standard applied consistently.
citations: IPC-1782 standard for manufacturing data; ASME Y14.38 abbreviations for parts lists.

name: Configurable and Variant BoMs
title: Configurable and Variant BoMs
description: Configurable BoMs describe product families with options (color, size, features) using rules instead of one BoM per variant. Variant BoMs are the resolved outputs: the exact parts list for one specific configuration.
how_it_works: Define option rules (if feature X then include part Y, exclude part Z) and validate that every legal combination resolves to a complete, buildable BoM. Test the extremes - all options on, all off, and each option alone.
key_points: One configurable BoM can serve hundreds of product variants.
Rules resolve options into variant-specific BoMs.
Validate every legal combination, especially the extremes.
Forbid illegal combinations in the rules, not in tribal knowledge.
requirements: A defined product structure with unique part numbers for every item; quantities and units of measure; revision control on the BoM document.
standards: IPC-1782 and IPC-2581 for electronics BoMs; ASME Y14.38 for parts lists; company part-numbering standard applied consistently.

name: Phantom Assemblies
title: Phantom Assemblies
description: A phantom assembly is a logical grouping that is never stocked or built separately - it exists only to organize the BoM. It simplifies kitting and documentation without adding inventory transactions.
how_it_works: Mark phantoms clearly in the BoM structure and configure your MRP system to blow through them (treat children as direct requirements of the parent). Use them for documentation groupings, not for things that will ever be inventoried.
key_points: Phantoms organize the BoM without creating stock transactions.
MRP must blow through phantoms to plan the real parts.
Never stock, cost, or schedule a phantom as a real assembly.
Use for documentation groupings like fastener kits or wiring groups.
requirements: A defined product structure with unique part numbers for every item; quantities and units of measure; revision control on the BoM document.
standards: IPC-1782 and IPC-2581 for electronics BoMs; ASME Y14.38 for parts lists; company part-numbering standard applied consistently.

name: BoM Cost Roll-Up
title: BoM Cost Roll-Up
description: Cost roll-up multiplies each line's quantity by its unit cost and sums upward through the levels to give the product's material cost. It is the foundation of pricing, margin analysis, and make-vs-buy decisions.
how_it_works: Attach current unit costs to every line (purchased price or computed make cost), roll up level by level, and separate material, labor, and overhead. Re-roll whenever costs or the BoM change - stale costs decide badly.
key_points: Extended cost = quantity-per-assembly x unit cost, summed per level.
Roll up from the lowest level to the top for the true material cost.
Keep material, labor, and overhead visible separately.
Re-roll costs on every BoM revision and every price change.
requirements: A defined product structure with unique part numbers for every item; quantities and units of measure; revision control on the BoM document.
standards: IPC-1782 and IPC-2581 for electronics BoMs; ASME Y14.38 for parts lists; company part-numbering standard applied consistently.
citations: IPC-1782 standard for manufacturing data; ASME Y14.38 abbreviations for parts lists.

name: Approved Vendor Lists on the BoM
title: Approved Vendor Lists on the BoM
description: An approved vendor list (AVL) names which suppliers are qualified for each part. Tying the AVL to BoM lines prevents purchasing from substituting unqualified sources when prices or lead times shift.
how_it_works: Record one or more approved vendors per line with their part numbers, and mark single-source lines as risks. Require engineering approval before any unlisted vendor is used on a released BoM.
key_points: Each BoM line can carry its approved vendors and their part numbers.
Single-source lines are flagged as supply risks.
Unlisted vendors require engineering approval before use.
Keep vendor part numbers cross-referenced to internal part numbers.

name: Where-Used Analysis
title: Where-Used Analysis
description: Where-used analysis answers the reverse question: which products and assemblies use this part? It is essential for change impact (what breaks if this part changes), obsolescence response, and recall scoping.
how_it_works: Maintain parent-child links in both directions so any part can be traced upward to every assembly and product. Run where-used before approving any part change, discontinuation, or substitution.
key_points: Where-used traces a part upward to every parent assembly and product.
Run it before any part change, substitution, or discontinuation.
It scopes recalls, field fixes, and obsolescence redesigns.
Requires the BoM stored as linked structure, not flat text.
requirements: A defined product structure with unique part numbers for every item; quantities and units of measure; revision control on the BoM document.
standards: IPC-1782 and IPC-2581 for electronics BoMs; ASME Y14.38 for parts lists; company part-numbering standard applied consistently.
